claim: Lactic acidosis could effectively protect cancer cells against glucose starvation or deprivation.
source: We recently found that Lactic acidosis could effectively protect cancer cells against glucose starvation or deprivaiton (Wu et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research publications (Wu et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2014).

claim: Lactic acidosis dramatically reduces glycolysis rate with little wasting glucose to lactate.
source: First, lactic acidosis dramatically reduces glycolysis rate with little wasting glucose to lactate, as such, a limited amount of glucose could support cancer cells for a relatively long time otherwise would be exhausted quickly.
evidence: The claim is based on previous research findings referenced in the context (Wu et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2014).

claim: When glucose was deprived, lactic acidosis transformed cancer cells to a 'dormant' state.
source: Second, when glucose was deprived, lactic acidosis transformed cancer cells to a 'dormant' state, via arresting cells at G0/G1 phase, initiating autophagy, inhibiting apoptosis, etc.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Wu et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2014).

claim: The protective function of lactic acidosis relies on co-presence of lactate and proton.
source: The protective function relies on co-presence of lactate and proton, depriving either of which would abolish the function (Wu et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research publications.

claim: When converting lactic acidosis to lactosis by a base, the protective function is gone.
source: When converting lactic acidosis to lactosis by a base, the protective function is gone; similarly, removing lactate, acidosis conferred cancer cells with little resistance to glucose deprivation.
evidence: The claim is based on previous research findings (Wu et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2014).

claim: High level of lactate was a strong prognostic indicator of increased metastasis and poor overall survival.
source: Clinical studies showed that high level of lactate was a strong prognostic indicator of increased metastasis and poor overall survival (Gatenby and Gillies, 2004; Brizel et al., 2001; Walenta et al., 2000; Schwickert et al., 1995; Walenta et al., 1997; Yokota et al., 2007; Paschen et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Systematic and tumor pHe alkalization could inhibit carcinogenesis, tumor invasion and metastasis.
source: The work of Gillies and Gatenby group demonstrated that systematic and tumor pHe alkalization could inhibit carcinogenesis, tumor invasion and metastasis, and they also provided integrated models that can predict the safety and efficacy of buffer therapy to raise tumour pHe (Silva et al., 2009; Robey et al., 2009; Ibrahim-Hashim et al., 2012) and related theoretical work (Martin et al., 2012, Martin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research by Gillies and Gatenby group.

claim: Lactic acidosis played multifaceted roles in skewing macrophages.
source: Furthermore, many studies reported that lactic acidosis played multifaceted roles in skewing macrophages (Colegio et al., 2014) and inhibiting the function of cytotoxic T cells (Haas et al., 2015), altering cancer cell metabolism (Chen et al., 2008; Sonveaux et al., 2008), inducing chromosomal instability (Dai et al., 2013), and promoting tumor angiogenesis (Gatenby and Gillies, 2004; Végran et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Colegio et al., 2014.

claim: Lactic acidosis inhibits the function of cytotoxic T cells.
source: Furthermore, many studies reported that lactic acidosis played multifaceted roles in skewing macrophages (Colegio et al., 2014) and inhibiting the function of cytotoxic T cells (Haas et al., 2015), altering cancer cell metabolism (Chen et al., 2008; Sonveaux et al., 2008), inducing chromosomal instability (Dai et al., 2013), and promoting tumor angiogenesis (Gatenby and Gillies, 2004; Végran et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Haas et al., 2015.

claim: Lactic acidosis alters cancer cell metabolism.
source: Furthermore, many studies reported that lactic acidosis played multifaceted roles in skewing macrophages (Colegio et al., 2014) and inhibiting the function of cytotoxic T cells (Haas et al., 2015), altering cancer cell metabolism (Chen et al., 2008; Sonveaux et al., 2008), inducing chromosomal instability (Dai et al., 2013), and promoting tumor angiogenesis (Gatenby and Gillies, 2004; Végran et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2008 and Sonveaux et al., 2008.

claim: Lactic acidosis induces chromosomal instability.
source: Furthermore, many studies reported that lactic acidosis played multifaceted roles in skewing macrophages (Colegio et al., 2014) and inhibiting the function of cytotoxic T cells (Haas et al., 2015), altering cancer cell metabolism (Chen et al., 2008; Sonveaux et al., 2008), inducing chromosomal instability (Dai et al., 2013), and promoting tumor angiogenesis (Gatenby and Gillies, 2004; Végran et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dai et al., 2013.

claim: Lactic acidosis promotes tumor angiogenesis.
source: Furthermore, many studies reported that lactic acidosis played multifaceted roles in skewing macrophages (Colegio et al., 2014) and inhibiting the function of cytotoxic T cells (Haas et al., 2015), altering cancer cell metabolism (Chen et al., 2008; Sonveaux et al., 2008), inducing chromosomal instability (Dai et al., 2013), and promoting tumor angiogenesis (Gatenby and Gillies, 2004; Végran et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gatenby and Gillies, 2004 and Végran et al., 2011.

claim: HCC larger than 3 cm in diameter is not suitable for curative therapy according to BCLC guideline.
source: According to the guideline of Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging and treatment strategy, HCC larger than 3 cm in diameter is not suitable for curative therapy (surgical resection, liver transplantation, and ablation) and the recommended treatment is TACE (Forner et al., 2012; El-Serag, 2011; Knox et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to BCLC guidelines (Forner et al., 2012; El-Serag, 2011; Knox et al., 2015).

claim: TACE is not effective to treat large tumors.
source: But sadly, it is recognized that TACE is not effective to treat large tumors (Sieghart et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sieghart et al., 2015.

claim: TACE kills HCC via delivering concentrated anticancer drugs locally into tumor and occluding tumor feeding arteries to deprive nutrients to starve cancer cells.
source: TACE kills HCC via 2 mechanisms, delivering concentrated anticancer drugs locally into tumor and occluding tumor feeding arteries to deprive nutrients to starve cancer cells.
evidence: The claim describes established mechanisms of TACE treatment.

claim: Embolization-created hypoxia condition would stimulate cancer cells to emit strong signals to initiate angiogenesis.
source: The problem is that embolization-created hypoxia condition would stimulate cancer cells to emit strong signals to initiate angiogenesis (Knox et al., 2015) to reestablish tumor vasculature to bypass the occluded tumor feeding arteries.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Knox et al., 2015.

claim: The lactate concentrations in HCC biopsies were around 20 mM.
source: The lactate concentrations in HCC biopsies were around 20 mM (unpublished data), suggesting a lactic acidosis condition.
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: In the nonrandomized study, the geometric mean of VTR in TACE with bicarbonate was 6.4-fold lower than that in TACE without bicarbonate.
source: In the nonrandomized controlled study, geometric mean of viable tumor residues (VTR) in TACE with bicarbonate was 6.4-fold lower than that in TACE without bicarbonate (7.1% [95% CI: 4.6%–10.9%] vs 45.6% [28.9%–72.0%]; p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the nonrandomized study presented in the abstract.

claim: TACE combined with bicarbonate yielded a 100% objective response rate in the nonrandomized study.
source: TACE combined with bicarbonate yielded a 100% objective response rate (ORR), whereas the ORR treated with TACE alone was 44.4% (nonrandomized) and 63.6% (randomized).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the nonrandomized study presented in the abstract.

claim: The ORR treated with TACE alone was 44.4% in the nonrandomized study.
source: TACE combined with bicarbonate yielded a 100% objective response rate (ORR), whereas the ORR treated with TACE alone was 44.4% (nonrandomized) and 63.6% (randomized).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the nonrandomized study presented in the abstract.

claim: The ORR treated with TACE alone was 63.6% in the randomized study.
source: TACE combined with bicarbonate yielded a 100% objective response rate (ORR), whereas the ORR treated with TACE alone was 44.4% (nonrandomized) and 63.6% (randomized).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the randomized study presented in the abstract.

claim: Bicarbonate may bring survival benefit.
source: The survival data suggested that bicarbonate may bring survival benefit.
evidence: The claim is based on survival data analysis presented in the abstract, but is stated cautiously as a suggestion.

claim: Bicarbonate markedly enhances the anticancer activity of TACE.
source: Conclusions:Bicarbonate markedly enhances the anticancer activity of TACE.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion drawn from the study data.

claim: Twenty-seven patients with large HCC were treated with cTACE in the nonrandomized study.
source: We retrieved 27 patients with large HCC (ranging 5.0–14.6 cm) from the pool of patients treated with cTACE in the hospital between 2010 and 2012 according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria as specified in the Materials and methods section.
evidence: The claim describes the study design and patient enrollment.

claim: Thirty patients were recruited for the TILA-TACE group in the nonrandomized study.
source: We then recruited 30 patients for the TILA-TACE group using the same inclusion and exclusion criteria between 2012 and 2013.
evidence: The claim describes the study design and patient enrollment.

claim: Most of patients' demographic and clinicopathologic characteristics between the two treatment groups cTACE and TILA-TACE were generally comparable in the nonrandomized study.
source: Most of patients' demographic and clinicopathologic characteristics between the two treatment groups cTACE and TILA-TACE were generally comparable (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Patients in the cTACE group were more likely to have multifocal tumors in the nonrandomized study.
source: However, patients in the cTACE group were more likely to have multifocal tumors.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of patient characteristics between groups.

claim: The geometric mean of VTR after the first treatment was 45.1% (95% CI: 30.3%–67.0%) in the cTACE group in the nonrandomized study.
source: The geometric mean of VTR after the first treatment was 45.1% (95% CI: 30.3%–67.0%) in the cTACE group, significantly greater than that in the TILA-TACE (7.1% [95% CI: 4.4%–11.5%]; p<0.0001) (Table 2 and Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data presented in Table 2 and Figure 1.

claim: The geometric mean of VTR after the first treatment was 7.1% (95% CI: 4.4%–11.5%) in the TILA-TACE group in the nonrandomized study.
source: The geometric mean of VTR after the first treatment was 45.1% (95% CI: 30.3%–67.0%) in the cTACE group, significantly greater than that in the TILA-TACE (7.1% [95% CI: 4.4%–11.5%]; p<0.0001) (Table 2 and Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data presented in Table 2 and Figure 1.

claim: The difference in VTR between cTACE and TILA-TACE groups was statistically significant (p<0.0001) in the nonrandomized study.
source: The geometric mean of VTR after the first treatment was 45.1% (95% CI: 30.3%–67.0%) in the cTACE group, significantly greater than that in the TILA-TACE (7.1% [95% CI: 4.4%–11.5%]; p<0.0001) (Table 2 and Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: None of the clinical covariates were significantly associated with VTR in the nonrandomized study.
source: In this study, none of these clinical covariates were significantly associated with VTR (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of covariates.

claim: TILA-TACE achieved a 81.1% therapeutic improvement relative to cTACE in the nonrandomized study.
source: TILA-TACE achieved a 81.1% therapeutic improvement relative to cTACE.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from VTR data.

claim: The percentage of CR, PR, SD, and PD in the cTACE group was 0%, 44.4%, 33.3%, and 22.2%, respectively, in the nonrandomized study.
source: The percentage of CR, PR, SD, and PD in the cTACE group was 0%, 44.4%, 33.3%, and 22.2% (Figure 2A), respectively, compared with 23%, 77%, 0%, and 0%, respectively, in the TILA-TACE group (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The percentage of CR, PR, SD, and PD in the TILA-TACE group was 23%, 77%, 0%, and 0%, respectively, in the nonrandomized study.
source: The percentage of CR, PR, SD, and PD in the cTACE group was 0%, 44.4%, 33.3%, and 22.2% (Figure 2A), respectively, compared with 23%, 77%, 0%, and 0%, respectively, in the TILA-TACE group (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The total objective response rate in the cTACE group was 44.4% in the nonrandomized study.
source: The total objective response rate (complete or partial responses) in the cTACE group was 44.4%, whereas it was 100% in the TILA-TACE group (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The total objective response rate in the TILA-TACE group was 100% in the nonrandomized study.
source: The total objective response rate (complete or partial responses) in the cTACE group was 44.4%, whereas it was 100% in the TILA-TACE group (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The observed greater responses to treatment in the TILA-TACE than in the cTACE persisted after accounting for tumor volume prior to treatment (p<0.0001) in the nonrandomized study.
source: The observed greater responses to treatment in the TILA-TACE than in the cTACE persisted after accounting for tumor volume prior to treatment using the proportional odds model (p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using proportional odds model.

claim: When patient number was 10 for each group, the estimated power value reached 0.826 for the RCT.
source: When patient number was 10 for each group, the estimated power value reached 0.826.
evidence: The claim is based on power calculation for the RCT sample size.

claim: Twenty patients with large HCC (5.0 – 13.5 cm) were randomly assigned into cTACE (n=10) or TILA-TACE (n=10) in 2014.
source: In 2014, we recruited and randomly assigned twenty patients with large HCC (5.0 – 13.5 cm) into cTACE (n=10) or TILA-TACE (n=10).
evidence: The claim describes the RCT study design and patient enrollment.

claim: Most of the selected clinicopathologic characteristics were well matched between two treatment groups in the RCT.
source: Again, most of the selected clinicopathologic characteristics were well matched between two treatment groups (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 3.

claim: After completion of the first treatment, the VTR in the TILA-TACE group was 5.5-fold lower than that in the cTACE group in the RCT.
source: After completion of the first treatment, the VTR in the TILA-TACE group was 5.5-fold lower than that in the cTACE group (4.6% [95% CI: 1.8%–11.4%] vs. 25.4% [95% CI: 10.1%–64.0%]; p=0.008) (Figure 3 and Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data presented in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: Only viable tumor volume before treatment was significantly associated with VTR in the RCT.
source: Among them, only viable tumor volume before treatment was significantly associated with VTR.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of covariates in the RCT.

claim: After adjustment for tumor volume before treatment, the VTR in the TILA-TACE was 4.1% (2.0%–8.4%) vs. 28.1% (13.9%–56.8%) in the cTACE (p=0.0009) in the RCT.
source: Adjustment for tumor volume before treatment slightly changed the results, with the VTR in the TILA-TACE of 4.1% (2.0%–8.4%) vs. 28.1% (13.9%–56.8%) in the cTACE (p=0.0009).
evidence: The claim is supported by adjusted statistical analysis.

claim: The relative therapeutic improvement by bicarbonate in the RCT was 80.1%.
source: The relative therapeutic improvement by bicarbonate in the RCT was 80.1%, similar to that observed in the non-randomized cohort, 81.1%.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from VTR data in the RCT.

claim: In TILA-TACE group, out of 12 targeted tumors, 4 achieved CR and 8 PR in the RCT.
source: If assessed by tumor objective response rate according to the EASL criteria, in TILA-TACE group, out of 12 targeted tumors, 4 achieved CR and 8 PR (Figure 4), whereas in cTACE group, out of 11 targeted tumors, 1 achieved CR, 6 PR, 2 SD, and 2 PD (Figure 4), with P value of 0.003 after adjustment for tumor volume prior to treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In cTACE group, out of 11 targeted tumors, 1 achieved CR, 6 PR, 2 SD, and 2 PD in the RCT.
source: If assessed by tumor objective response rate according to the EASL criteria, in TILA-TACE group, out of 12 targeted tumors, 4 achieved CR and 8 PR (Figure 4), whereas in cTACE group, out of 11 targeted tumors, 1 achieved CR, 6 PR, 2 SD, and 2 PD (Figure 4), with P value of 0.003 after adjustment for tumor volume prior to treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The difference in tumor response between TILA-TACE and cTACE groups was statistically significant (p=0.003) after adjustment for tumor volume prior to treatment in the RCT.
source: If assessed by tumor objective response rate according to the EASL criteria, in TILA-TACE group, out of 12 targeted tumors, 4 achieved CR and 8 PR (Figure 4), whereas in cTACE group, out of 11 targeted tumors, 1 achieved CR, 6 PR, 2 SD, and 2 PD (Figure 4), with P value of 0.003 after adjustment for tumor volume prior to treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The ORR in TILA-TACE group was 100% in the RCT.
source: In this RCT, the ORR in TILA-TACE group was 100% and the ORR in cTACE group was 63.6%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the RCT.

claim: The ORR in cTACE group was 63.6% in the RCT.
source: In this RCT, the ORR in TILA-TACE group was 100% and the ORR in cTACE group was 63.6%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the RCT.

claim: The 1-, 2-, 3-year survival of 27 patients treated with cTACE were 66.7% (95% CI 45.7%–81.1%), 40.7% (95% CI 22.5%–58.2%), and 25.9% (95% CI 11.5%–43.1%), respectively, in the nonrandomized study.
source: In the nonrandomized cohort of study, the 1-, 2-, 3-year survival of 27 patients treated with cTACE retrieved from our database were 66.7% (95% CI 45.7%–81.1%), 40.7% (95% CI 22.5%–58.2%), and 25.9% (95% CI 11.5%–43.1%), respectively, with a median survival of 14 months (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The median survival of patients treated with cTACE was 14 months in the nonrandomized study.
source: In the nonrandomized cohort of study, the 1-, 2-, 3-year survival of 27 patients treated with cTACE retrieved from our database were 66.7% (95% CI 45.7%–81.1%), 40.7% (95% CI 22.5%–58.2%), and 25.9% (95% CI 11.5%–43.1%), respectively, with a median survival of 14 months (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The 1-, 2-, 3-year survival of 30 patients treated with TILA-TACE were 82.8% (95% CI 63.4%–92.8%), 67.7% (95% CI 47.0%–81.8%), and 61.8% (95% CI 39.7%–77.8%), respectively, in the nonrandomized study.
source: and the 1-, 2-, 3-year survival of 30 patients treated with TILA-TACE were 82.8% (95% CI 63.4%–92.8%), 67.7% (95% CI 47.0%–81.8%), and 61.8% (95% CI 39.7%–77.8%), respectively, with a median survival beyond 41 months (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The median survival of patients treated with TILA-TACE was beyond 41 months in the nonrandomized study.
source: and the 1-, 2-, 3-year survival of 30 patients treated with TILA-TACE were 82.8% (95% CI 63.4%–92.8%), 67.7% (95% CI 47.0%–81.8%), and 61.8% (95% CI 39.7%–77.8%), respectively, with a median survival beyond 41 months (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The survival difference between TILA-TACE and cTACE was statistically significant (p=0.0052) in the nonrandomized study.
source: The survival difference between TILA-TACE and cTACE was statistically significant (p=0.0052).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Four patients initially assigned in and treated with cTACE group subsequently requested to cross over to TILA-TACE treatment in the RCT.
source: In the randomized study, 4 patients initially assigned in and treated with cTACE group subsequently requested to cross over to TILA-TACE treatment.
evidence: The claim describes what happened during the RCT.

claim: In cTACE group, 3 deaths occurred in 6 patients who solely received cTACE treatment in the RCT.
source: In cTACE group, 3 deaths occurred in 6 patients who solely received cTACE treatment, and 4 patients who initially received cTACE treatment and subsequently crossed over to TILA-TACE treatment were alive.
evidence: The claim is based on survival data from the RCT.

claim: Four patients who initially received cTACE treatment and subsequently crossed over to TILA-TACE treatment were alive in the RCT.
source: In cTACE group, 3 deaths occurred in 6 patients who solely received cTACE treatment, and 4 patients who initially received cTACE treatment and subsequently crossed over to TILA-TACE treatment were alive.
evidence: The claim is based on survival data from the RCT.

claim: In TILA-TACE group of 10 patients, 3 deaths occurred and 7 patients live in the RCT.
source: In TILA-TACE group of 10 patients, 3 deaths occurred and 7 patients live.
evidence: The claim is based on survival data from the RCT.

claim: There was no apparent difference in overall survival between two treatment groups in the intent-to-treat (ITT) analysis in the RCT.
source: There was no apparent difference in overall survival between two treatment groups in the intent-to-treat (ITT) analysis (Figure 5B, left panel).
evidence: The claim is based on ITT survival analysis presented in Figure 5B.

claim: A survival advantage appears in TILA-TACE treatment over cTACE treatment in the per-protocol (PP) analysis, but statistically not significant in the RCT.
source: However, a survival advantage appears in TILA-TACE treatment over cTACE treatment in the per-protocol (PP) analysis (Figure 5B, right panel), but statistically not significant.
evidence: The claim is based on PP survival analysis presented in Figure 5B.

claim: After pooling all patients together, there was a significant difference of survival between cTACE and TILA-TACE group.
source: After pooling all patients together, there was a significant difference of survival between cTACE and TILA-TACE group (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on pooled survival analysis presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The adverse effect between cTACE and TILA-TACE group were comparable.
source: The adverse effect between cTACE and TILA-TACE group were comparable (Tables 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by adverse event data presented in Tables 5 and 6.

claim: The numbers reflecting the therapeutic improvements by TILA-TACE from the 2 studies were nearly identical (81.1% and 80.1%).
source: The most striking point is that the numbers reflecting the therapeutic improvements by TILA-TACE from the 2 studies were nearly identical (81.1% and 80.1%).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of therapeutic improvement calculations from both studies.

claim: The average objective tumor response to TACE is 35% (range, 16%–61%).
source: The average objective tumor response to TACE is 35% (range, 16%–61%), as systematically reviewed by LIovet and Bruix for the Barcelona-Clinic Liver Cancer Group in 2002 (Llovet and Bruix, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a systematic review by Llovet and Bruix, 2003.

claim: More than 50% of patients had an objective response to TACE according to a 2012 summary.
source: In 2012, Forner, LIovet, and Bruix summarized that more than 50% of patients had an objective response to TACE (Forner et al., 2012), suggesting that the objective tumor response to TACE in the 10-year period (2002–2012) had been increased for about 15%.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Forner et al., 2012.

claim: The complete tumor response to TACE is rare (0-4.8%).
source: The complete tumor response to TACE is rare (0-4.8%) (Jansen et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jansen et al., 2005.

claim: Better local control was an independent prognostic indicator for patient survival.
source: Many previous studies have confirmed that better local control was an independent prognostic indicator for patient survival (Kim et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2013; Shim et al., 2012; Riaz et al., 2011; Gillmore et al., 2011; Riaz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Kim et al and Shim et al demonstrated a clear prognostic difference between CR, PR, stable disease and progressive disease.
source: Kim et al and Shim et al (Kim et al., 2015; Shim et al., 2012) further demonstrated a clear prognostic difference between CR, PR, stable disease and progressive disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2015 and Shim et al., 2012.

claim: TILA-TACE achieved a remarkable improvement of local tumor control.
source: The current study demonstrated that TILA-TACE achieved a remarkable improvement of local tumor control and suggested an early sign of improved survival for patients with large HCCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on the study results presented in the manuscript.

claim: TILA-TACE suggested an early sign of improved survival for patients with large HCCs.
source: The current study demonstrated that TILA-TACE achieved a remarkable improvement of local tumor control and suggested an early sign of improved survival for patients with large HCCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on survival data presented in Figure 5A, but stated cautiously as a suggestion.

claim: During follow up, 16 patients in the TILA-TACE arm eventually exhibited progressive disease.
source: It is noted that, during follow up, 16 patients in the TILA-TACE arm (Figure 5A), eventually exhibited progressive disease, including 11 patients with new foci in the liver, 1 with new liver foci and lung metastasis, and 3 with lung metastasis, and 1 with bone metastasis, all of which may account for the death (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on follow-up data from the study.

claim: Fast CR and timely control of recurrent tumors in the liver would likely improve the survival of patients, especially those with large tumor burden and low liver reserve.
source: These observations suggest that fast CR and timely control of recurrent tumors in the liver would likely improve the survival of patients, especially those with large tumor burden and low liver reserve.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observations of progressive disease.

claim: The randomized controlled study designed in this investigation was for local tumor control, not for survival.
source: The randomized controlled study designed in this investigation was for local tumor control, not for survival.
evidence: The claim describes the study design.

claim: The small sample size of the RCT did not allow for statistically significant data for cumulative survival.
source: Although the small sample size allowed us to evaluate the local tumor control, we did not expect that such small sample size would yield statistically significant data for cumulative survival.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: There are many more factors affecting the survival of patients than those affecting the local tumor control.
source: Evaluation of survival is a matter much more complicated than evaluation of local control. There are many more factors affecting the survival of patients than those affecting the local tumor control, e.g., tumor characteristics, liver function reserve, tumor staging, disease complications, vascular invasion, metastasis, etc., all of which must be well controlled.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about cancer survival factors.

claim: The RCT was limited by the small sample size.
source: Overall, the RCT was limited by the small sample size and the result of the PP analysis was potentially confounded by the crossover of patients from cTACE group to TILA-TACE.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: The result of the PP analysis was potentially confounded by the crossover of patients from cTACE group to TILA-TACE.
source: Overall, the RCT was limited by the small sample size and the result of the PP analysis was potentially confounded by the crossover of patients from cTACE group to TILA-TACE.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: TILA-TACE was as tolerable as cATCE.
source: There was no significant difference of adverse effect between TILA-TACE and cTACE (Tables 3 and 4), i.e., TILA-TACE was as tolerable as cATCE.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of adverse events data.

claim: Locally administration of bicarbonate into tumor is safe.
source: It was within our expectation, as locally administration of bicarbonate into tumor is safe.
evidence: The claim is based on the observed safety profile in the study.

claim: Bicarbonate infusion locally into HCC can markedly enhance anticancer activity of TACE.
source: Taken together, this pilot study demonstrated that bicarbonate infusion locally into HCC can markedly enhance anticancer activity of TACE, supporting the notion that neutralizing intratumoral lactic acidosis combined with glucose deprivation may deliver an effective approach to control tumor.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion drawn from the study data.

claim: Neutralizing intratumoral lactic acidosis combined with glucose deprivation may deliver an effective approach to control tumor.
source: Taken together, this pilot study demonstrated that bicarbonate infusion locally into HCC can markedly enhance anticancer activity of TACE, supporting the notion that neutralizing intratumoral lactic acidosis combined with glucose deprivation may deliver an effective approach to control tumor.
evidence: The claim is a broader conclusion supported by the study findings.

claim: The study was performed with patients' written informed consent and with the approval of hospital's Institutional Review Board.
source: The study was performed with patients' written informed consent and with the approval of hospital's Institutional Review Board.
